title: In the Depth of Night
intro: Hamza al-Malik Tumbul called this meditation “In the Depth of Night” in his Diwan al-Tabi'a. Human eyes close in sleep, while the eyes of the stars remain open above a world of human strife. Osama Al-Waaedh takes verses three and four and repeats the fourth, lingering over a question that the longer poem pursues into the waking lives of people. In the recitation the watching stars look towards one person.

translation: They gaze at me, all unmindful
1.sharh: The eyes belong to the stars in the preceding, unrecited verse. They stay open while human eyes sleep, yet seem untouched by the world they look down on.

translation: of God that holds them spellbound, or the passing of the centuries?
2.sharh: He wonders whether the stars are lost in the sight of divine majesty or in the sheer duration of what they have witnessed. The reciter gives the question a second hearing.

1.1.1.head: رَنا
1.1.1.meaning: Gazes steadily. The eyes of the stars, named immediately before this excerpt, are the subject.

1.1.2.meaning: “At me”, as recited. The printed collection has “at us”.

1.1.4.head: سالِيَة
1.1.4.meaning: Untroubled, having put something out of mind. The word continues in the next half. The print reads sahiya, heedless.

1.2.4.head: الخَؤون
1.2.4.meaning: Habitually treacherous, said of a world that repeatedly betrays trust.

2.1.2.head: أَذهَلَ
2.1.2.meaning: Left them absorbed or distracted. The pronoun refers back to the eyes.

2.1.3.head: جَلال
2.1.3.meaning: Majesty or awe-inspiring greatness. The l opening the next half completes the word.

2.2.4-5.head: مَرُّ القُرون
2.2.4-5.meaning: “The passage of the ages”: a second possible cause of the stars’ absorption.
